objects.name: Criminal Gang Active Directory Takeover – Canadian Energy Sector
objects.description: A financially-motivated criminal gang targets a mid-sized Canadian energy company (~2500 employees) with the objective of achieving full Active Directory compromise. The intrusion begins with a targeted phishing campaign against corporate users, establishes persistence via a commodity RAT or implant, then pivots through credential theft and lateral movement to reach a Domain Controller. The AD takeover enables ransomware staging or data extortion. Pattern is consistent with Black Basta, LockBit, and Akira affiliate activity observed against North American energy and utilities organisations.

objects.name: Spearphishing Link – Credential Harvesting Portal
objects.description: Attackers send targeted phishing emails impersonating an IT helpdesk or O365 sign-in notification to energy sector employees. The link redirects to an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) proxy page that captures credentials and session cookies, bypassing MFA. Observed in Akira and Black Basta campaigns against Canadian critical infrastructure.

objects.name: Valid Account – Use of Harvested Employee Credentials
objects.description: Using credentials and session tokens captured via the AiTM phish, the attacker authenticates to the victim's Microsoft 365 / Azure AD tenant and VPN portal as a legitimate domain user. No malware is dropped at this stage; the actor appears as normal user activity.

objects.name: Remote Services – VPN / RDP into Corporate Network
objects.description: The threat actor uses the compromised credentials to authenticate to the corporate SSL-VPN or publically exposed RDP gateway, gaining a foothold inside the on-premises network segment that houses OT-adjacent systems and the AD infrastructure.

objects.name: OS Credential Dumping – LSASS Memory
objects.description: Once on an internal Windows host, the attacker uses a credential-dumping tool (e.g., Mimikatz, Nanodump) to extract NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets from LSASS memory. This yields service account and potentially privileged credentials needed for lateral movement.

objects.name: Domain Account & Group Enumeration
objects.description: The attacker runs BloodHound / SharpHound or native LDAP queries to map AD group memberships, identify privileged accounts (Domain Admins, Backup Operators), delegation paths, and shortest paths to Domain Controller. Widely used in ransomware pre-staging.

objects.name: Kerberoasting – Service Account Ticket Extraction
objects.description: Using the BloodHound-identified service accounts with SPNs (common in energy companies for SCADA/historian integrations), the attacker requests Kerberos TGS tickets offline and cracks weak passwords to obtain higher-privileged service account credentials.

objects.name: Lateral Movement – Pass-the-Hash / Pass-the-Ticket to Privileged Hosts
objects.description: Using NTLM hashes dumped from LSASS and cracked Kerberoast tickets, the attacker authenticates laterally to IT admin workstations and jump servers without needing cleartext passwords. This progression targets systems with Domain Admin logon sessions.

objects.name: Scheduled Task / Service Persistence on Beachhead Host
objects.description: On the compromised admin workstation or member server, the attacker installs a scheduled task running a C2 beacon (Cobalt Strike or Brute Ratel) to maintain access independent of the original VPN session. This ensures re-entry if credentials are reset.

objects.name: DCSync – Replication of All Domain Credentials
objects.description: With Domain Admin or equivalent privileges gained via lateral movement, the attacker performs a DCSync operation (using secretsdump or Mimikatz lsadump::dcsync) to replicate the NTDS.dit contents, extracting KRBTGT hash and all domain account hashes. This constitutes full AD compromise.

objects.name: Golden Ticket Forging – Persistent Privileged Access
objects.description: Using the extracted KRBTGT hash, the attacker forges a Golden Ticket Kerberos TGT granting arbitrary domain access for an extended validity period (typically 10 years). This persists even after a password reset of compromised accounts unless the KRBTGT is rotated twice.

objects.name: Inhibit System Recovery – Disable VSS / Backup Services
objects.description: Pre-ransomware staging: the attacker uses AD-wide GPO or PSExec to disable Windows Volume Shadow Copy services, delete shadow copies, and disable backup agents across the estate — including any OT historian or SCADA management servers in scope. Consistent with Akira and Black Basta pre-detonation tradecraft.
